title: First Sea Fishing — National Day on the Coast
excerpt: Blue mackerel scad, rabbitfish, stolen bait, and a fisherman's wisdom: Go lighter.
body: During the National Day holiday I tried sea fishing for the first time. Luck was on my side — blue mackerel scad and rabbitfish, plus a sunset that made the wait worthwhile.

There's a different rhythm to life when you step away from the bench. Salt air replaces IPA, long silences replace the hum of instruments, and small victories are measured in centimetres of line rather than nanometres of interface. It's a different problem space entirely — and that's exactly why it resets something important.
Setting Out

The boat left the pier just after dawn. The water was still — a flat, grey-green sheet that barely moved. As we motored further from shore, the colour shifted: first turquoise where the sand held, then a deep navy as the shelf dropped away beneath us. By the time we cut the engine, land was a pencil line on the horizon.

I rigged up with too much weight — the kind of mistake you only make once. The sinker hit bottom immediately, and the line went slack. A few adjustments later, I had bait in the water and hope to spare.
The sea doesn't care about your credentials. Out here, you're a beginner like everyone else.
The Experience

The first hour was a masterclass in humility. My bait kept getting stripped clean — nibbled away by something too small to hook. I'd reel up bare hooks and repeat the cycle: bait, drop, wait, disappointment.
A seasoned fisherman on the boat had been watching. He walked over, inspected my rig, and offered the simplest advice: "They can feel the weight of your hook. Go lighter."
Three words, but they changed everything. I swapped the sinker for a smaller one, thinned the leader, and let the bait drift naturally. Within fifteen minutes, the rod tip dipped hard — and I was in.
The Catches

First came a blue mackerel scad, its flank catching the light like polished metal. Small, but fierce — it fought harder than anything its size had a right to. Then a rabbitfish, with its comically expressive face and venomous dorsal spines I'd been warned to avoid. A third followed, and by midday the esky had something worth showing.
Each strike brought the same rush: the sudden tension on the line, the rod bending into an arc, the instinct to reel too fast and the discipline to slow down. You learn quickly that panic costs fish.
What I Noticed
<ul>
• The water changes colour with depth — turquoise near shore, dark navy beyond the shelf
• Boats rock differently than lab benches, but the feeling of focused waiting is the same
• Good fishing is mostly patience — knowing when to act and when to let the bait sit
• The best advice comes from people who've been doing it longer than you've been alive

Research Echo
The fisherman's advice — "Go lighter" — is the same principle we arrived at with flexible bioelectronics. A rigid interface loses contact because it imposes its own structure rather than adapting to the tissue's. Whether you're hooking a fish or recording from an organoid, conformity beats force every time.
Why It Mattered

Research is a long game with ambiguous feedback. You spend months tuning a fabrication process, and the result is a line on a plot. Fishing, by contrast, gives you binary feedback: you either catch something or you don't. There's something restorative about a problem with an unambiguous success condition.

That said, the two aren't as different as they first appear. Both demand patience you don't always have. Both punish overeagerness. Both reward the person who watches carefully and adjusts incrementally rather than overhauling everything at once. The fisherman who tweaks his leader weight is doing the same thing as the researcher who dials in PDMS curing time.
Adapt or go home with empty hands. On the water and in the lab, the rule holds.
<hr>
Already planning the next trip. This time with lighter tackle and heavier expectations.
